This is drawn from a census taken in the last week of March 1991. Three months later the country in it began to come apart. Red is Catholic, blue Orthodox, green Muslim — and the middle is where they refuse to sort.

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ That census was Yugoslavia's last. In Bosnia it counted 4,377,033 people: 43.5% Muslims, 31.2% Serbs, 17.4% Croats. Nobody held a majority. That is the shattered middle of the map, in numbers.

2/ Look at how the edges behave. Slovenia and Croatia are solid red, Serbia and Montenegro solid blue. Bosnia is the seam where Latin and Orthodox Christianity met roughly a thousand years ago and never finished dividing.

3/ Bosnia's census covered 109 municipalities, and in dozens of them no group reached half. Sarajevo alone recorded 56,470 people who answered "Yugoslav" — about one in ten of the city, and an answer this map has no colour for.

4/ The green is the Ottoman layer. Kosovo, western Macedonia, and Sandžak — the Bosniak-majority region straddling southwest Serbia and eastern Montenegro, named after the Ottoman sanjak of Novi Pazar — are where that rule lasted longest.

5/ But Kosovo's colour is largely an estimate. Almost all Albanians boycotted the 1991 census after Ibrahim Rugova called for a boycott of Serbian institutions. The most evenly coloured corner of the map is the part nobody actually counted.

6/ The orange specks are the real surprise. In Vojvodina they are Slovak Lutherans, descended from families who left the Tatras in the 1700s to escape the Counter-Reformation. The patch in northeast Slovenia is Prekmurje, Lutheran since 1781.

7/ Read it as a forecast rather than an explanation. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. Where the colour was solid, the break took days. Where it interlocks, it took years.
